ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was not required because only published data were analyzed.

In PROGRESS, new permanent pacemakers were implanted in 17.3% vs 9.3% of patients without a pacemaker at baseline (80 more per 1,000; 95% CI: 28-132 more; number needed to harm 13; 95% CI: 8-36), whereas disabling stroke, myocardial infarction, life-threatening bleeding, and new atrial fibrillation did not differ significantly.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> In PROGRESS, new permanent pacemakers were implanted in 17.3% vs 9.3% of patients without a pacemaker at baseline (80 more per 1,000; 95% CI: 28-132 more; number needed to harm 13; 95% CI: 8-36), whereas disabling stroke, myocardial infarction, life-threatening bleeding, and new atrial fibrillation did not differ significantly.

Ethics approval statement:

> Ethical approval was not required because only published data were analyzed.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: With 2 trials, between-trial variance cannot be estimated reliably, so the primary model was common-effect (inverse variance for log HRs; Mantel-Haenszel for RRs). Random-effects models (restricted maximum likelihood with the modified Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman adjustment) were sensitivity analyses; 22 I² was reported but not used to decide whether to pool. 23 Absolute effects at 2 years applied the pooled relative effect to the PROGRESS surveillance-arm risk and, for death, also to the TAVR UNLOAD risk; numbers needed to treat or harm were rounded up. The optimal information size was the number of events needed to detect a 20% to 25% relative reduction with 80% power and a 2-sided α of 0.05, and trial sequential analysis with O'Brien-Fleming monitoring boundaries tested whether cumulative evidence was conclusive. 24 A Bayesian random-effects model (normal prior on the log HR with mean 0 and SD 1; half-normal prior on τ with scale 0.5, and 0.25 and 1.0 in sensitivity analyses) estimated the probability of benefit. 25 The intention-to-treat estimate was primary; crossover was tabulated, and crossover-censored estimates were reported as published. 26 Differences between trials, between subgroups within PROGRESS, and between the randomized and observational tiers were tested as ratios of relative effects, 27 and the credibility of effect modification was judged with ICEMAN. 28 TAVR UNLOAD did not report outcomes by sex.
table.statistical_test_other: trial sequential analysis with O'Brien-Fleming monitoring boundaries

table.text: Early TAVR did not detectably change all-cause death (2 trials, 126 deaths; HR: 1.05; 95% CI: 0.74-1.49; P = 0.80; I² = 0%) (Figure 1A). Truncated at a common 2-year horizon, the RR was 1.19 (95% CI: 0.83-1.71). At PROGRESS-like risk, this corresponds to 3 more deaths per 1,000 at 2 years (19 fewer to 34 more), and at TAVR UNLOAD-like risk to 9 more (54 fewer to 91 more). Detecting a 20% relative reduction with 80% power requires about 630 deaths; the trials provide one-fifth of that number, and the cumulative Z-curve (Z = 0.26) was far from any monitoring boundary.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.
